title: Dynamic types, coercion, and equality — interview

items.question: Why does typeof null return 'object'?
items.answer: In the original JavaScript implementation (Mocha engine), values were 32-bit tags plus payload. Zero represented both null and empty object references. The spec kept this behavior for backwards compatibility. `null` is a primitive, not an object. Always test with `value === null` before treating a value as an object.
followUps: How do you safely check for a plain object?
What does typeof return for arrays and functions?
items.sixtySeconds: typeof null is 'object' — legacy bug from engine tag bits. null is a primitive. Always use === null. typeof works for other primitives.

items.question: Explain the difference between == and ===.
items.answer: `===` uses Strict Equality Comparison — same type and value, no coercion. `==` uses Abstract Equality Comparison — it may convert types first (`'5' == 5` is true, `0 == false` is true, `null == undefined` is true). Modern code defaults to `===`. The one idiomatic `==` use is `x == null` to catch both null and undefined.
followUps: What is [] == ![] and why?
When would you use Object.is instead of ===?
items.sixtySeconds: === no coercion, same type required. == coerces — '5'==5 true. Default ===. Only == for x==null. Object.is for NaN and ±0.

items.question: What is SameValueZero and where is it used?
items.answer: SameValueZero is like `===` except NaN equals NaN and +0 equals -0. `Map` and `Set` use SameValueZero for key lookup — so `map.set(NaN, 'x')` and `map.get(NaN)` work. `Object.is` uses SameValue (NaN equals NaN but +0 !== -0). `Array.includes` uses SameValueZero; `indexOf` uses strict equality.
followUps: Why does NaN === NaN return false?
Does Array.indexOf find NaN?
items.sixtySeconds: SameValueZero: like === but NaN===NaN and +0===-0. Map/Set keys. Object.is distinguishes ±0. includes uses SameValueZero.

items.question: How does the + operator decide between concatenation and addition?
items.answer: If either operand is a primitive string (or becomes one after ToPrimitive), `+` converts both sides with ToString and concatenates. Otherwise it converts both with ToNumber and adds. That is why `'5' + 2` is `'52'` but `'5' - 2` is `3` (subtraction always uses ToNumber). Objects coerce via ToPrimitive (valueOf then toString) before the decision.
followUps: What does [] + [] evaluate to?
What is ToPrimitive?
items.sixtySeconds: + checks for string — concat if yes, else ToNumber add. Objects use ToPrimitive first. - always ToNumber.

items.question: List all falsy values in JavaScript.
items.answer: Exactly eight: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n` (BigInt zero), `''` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]`, and `{}`. Use `??` for nullish defaults (only null/undefined); use `||` only when any falsy should trigger a fallback.
followUps: Is an empty array falsy?
What is the difference between || and ??
items.sixtySeconds: Eight falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. [] is truthy. ?? for nullish only. || for any falsy.

items.question: When should you use BigInt instead of number?
items.answer: When you need integers beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2⁵³ − 1). Snowflake IDs, cryptographic values, and large counters lose precision as `number`. Use `bigint` literals with `n` suffix. BigInt cannot mix with `number` in arithmetic without explicit conversion. `JSON.stringify` throws on BigInt — serialize as string.
followUps: What is 9007199254740993 as a number?
Can you use Math.sqrt on a BigInt?
items.sixtySeconds: BigInt past 2⁵³-1. number rounds silently. 9007199254740993n exact. No mix with number. JSON needs string.

items.question: How is JavaScript dynamic typing different from TypeScript and C#?
items.answer: JavaScript checks types at run time — variables can hold any value. TypeScript adds compile-time static checks but erases all types when compiling to JavaScript — no run-time type safety. C# enforces types at compile time AND run time via the CLR — types survive in IL. At API boundaries, always validate `JSON.parse` results regardless of TypeScript.
followUps: Is C# var dynamically typed?
What is TypeScript unknown vs any?
items.sixtySeconds: JS dynamic at runtime. TS compile-only, erased. C# compile+CLR runtime. Validate JSON at boundaries always.

items.question: What are the security risks of JSON.parse?
items.answer: `JSON.parse` itself does not execute code (unlike `eval`). Risks are data-level: prototype pollution via `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype` keys when merging parsed objects into existing ones, and trusting unvalidated shape (wrong types causing logic bugs). Safe pattern: parse, validate with schema (Zod) or guards, reject dangerous keys, use `Object.create(null)` for dictionaries. Never use `eval` for JSON.
followUps: What does JSON.stringify do with undefined?
When would you use structuredClone instead of JSON?
items.sixtySeconds: JSON.parse safe from RCE but not data attacks. Block __proto__. Validate shape. No eval. structuredClone for memory clone.

items.question: What is the purpose of Symbol in JavaScript?
items.answer: Symbol creates unique, immutable primitive values — primarily for non-colliding object property keys and language protocol hooks (`Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.toStringTag`). Symbol keys are non-enumerable in `Object.keys`. `Symbol.for('key')` registers in a global registry for cross-module sharing. Each `Symbol('desc')` is unique even with the same description.
followUps: How do Symbol keys appear in JSON.stringify?
How do private class fields (#) compare to Symbol keys?
items.sixtySeconds: Symbol for unique keys and protocols. Non-enumerable. Symbol.for for shared registry. Not in JSON. Each Symbol() unique.

items.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in JavaScript?
items.answer: JavaScript `number` is IEEE 754 double-precision floating point — the same family as C# `double`. Decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary. `0.1 + 0.2` produces `0.30000000000000004`. For money, use integer cents or a decimal library — JavaScript has no `decimal` type like C#. Compare floats with epsilon or round explicitly.
followUps: What is Number.EPSILON used for?
How does C# decimal differ?
items.sixtySeconds: number is IEEE 754 double. 0.1+0.2 imprecision like C# double. Use integer cents or decimal library for money.
